On Wed, September 4, 2019 11:13 pm, Emmanuel Paul Wicker wrote:
>
> My next question : why does my fasta file contain sequences whose length
> is 281,141, whereas there should be 5,196 SNP positions ?

method = 1 means that all the bases from that fragment are included.  Thus
it is all the trimmed sequences.

If you only want the snp position then method = 3.

Check the help for an explanation of the options for method.  ?gl2fasta

Cheers
Peter

messages.body_plain:
Dear Everyone,

I'm trying to write gl objects into a .csv files by using the function:

gl.write.csv(testset.gl <http://testset.gl>, outfile="SNP_1row.csv")

I'm getting the following error:

Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE) :
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 188

Does anyone know how can I fix this error? I found the description of the function (below) just in case.
Thanks in advance for your help.
Monica

#' Write out data from a gl object \link{adegenet} to csv file
#'
#' This script writes to file the SNP genotypes with specimens as entities (columns) and
#' loci as attributes (rows). Each row has associated locus metadata. Each column, with header
#' of specimen id, has population in the first row.
#'
#' The data coding differs from the DArT 1 row format in that 0 = reference homozygous, 2 =
#' alternate homozygous, 1 = heterozyous, and NA = missing SNP assignment.
#'
#' @param gl -- name of the genlight object containing SNP genotypes [required]
#' @param outfile -- name of the csv file to write the data to [required]
#' @param outpath -- path where to save the output file (set to tempdir by default)
#' @return saves a glenlight object to csv
#' @export
#' @author Arthur Georges (bugs? Post to \url{https://groups.google.com/d/forum/dartr})
#' @examples
#' gl.write.csv(testset.gl <http://testset.gl>, outfile="SNP_1row.csv")

gl.write.csv <https://rdrr.io/cran/dartR/man/gl.write.csv.html> <- function <https://rdrr.io/r/base/function.html>(gl <https://rdrr.io/r/base/gl.html>, outfile="outfile.csv", outpath=tempdir <https://rdrr.io/r/base/tempfile.html>()) {

  outfile <- file.path <https://rdrr.io/r/base/file.path.html>(outpath, outfile)
  x <- gl <https://rdrr.io/r/base/gl.html>

# Add individual names and population names to rows
  x1 <- cbind.data.frame <https://rdrr.io/r/base/cbind.html>(pop(x),as.matrix <https://rdrr.io/r/base/matrix.html>(x))
# Transpose to have id as columns, loci as rows
  x1 <- t <https://rdrr.io/r/base/t.html>(x1)
# Create two filler rows to bring number of data rows and number of locus.metadata rows together
  filler1 <- rep <https://rdrr.io/r/base/rep.html>("*",length <https://rdrr.io/r/base/length.html>(x@other$loc.metrics[1,]))
# Bind the filler rows to the locus metadata
  x2 <- rbind <https://rdrr.io/r/base/cbind.html>(filler1, as.matrix <https://rdrr.io/r/base/matrix.html>(x@other$loc.metrics))
# Bind the locus metadata to the data
  x3 <- cbind.data.frame <https://rdrr.io/r/base/cbind.html>(x2,x1)
# Output
  write.table <https://rdrr.io/r/utils/write.table.html>(x3, file <https://rdrr.io/r/base/connections.html>=outfile,sep=",",row.names <https://rdrr.io/r/base/row.names.html>=FALSE <https://rdrr.io/r/base/logical.html>)

  a <- NULL <https://rdrr.io/r/base/NULL.html>
  return <https://rdrr.io/r/base/function.html>(a)
}

messages.subject: Interpretation of gl.diversity
messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of gl.diversity
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Thank you for developing what it's looking like a very comprehensive and integrative R package!
I have some questions regarding the interpretation of results from gl.diversity, which might just relate to my lack of understanding of the functions.

I calculated alpha and beta diversity for q=0, q=1 and q=2, and I'm now trying to interpret the data based on what is described in Sherwin et al. 2017.
I understand that for within population diversity, i.e. alpha values, q=0 represents allelic richness index, q=1 Shannon information index and q=2 heterozygosity index, and that these indices are represented by H values. These H values can then be converted to a common scale of effective numbers, D.
For between population comparisons of diversity, i.e. beta values, q=0 represents number of allelic types not shared between pops, q=1 measures the chance of a type of individuals providing info on the sampling locality, and q=2 measured the chance of two random individuals from different localities having different allelic types.
Please correct any of these if I'm wrong.

My question with beta diversity is that the supp material of Sherwin et al. 2017 provides many options to calculate each of these indices, and I'm not sure what the output from gl.diversity represents for each index. For example, Beta diversity for q=1 can represent the Mutual Information (I) or Shannon differentiation, but I'm not sure what is outputted. Do we get only calculations of H and D and we then need to calculate these measures a posteriori with a different function? Can we interpret H and D directly for both alpha and beta?

Any guidance would be most welcome.

Best,
Soraia

This function gives a PCoA plot showing my to which population belongs. Axis 1 (30.7%) and axis 2 (27%) explain more than 50% of the variation shown. In your previous reply you mentioned:

> If  Variety 1 and remainder have good separation on PCoA1 (and good value for variance explained), then you can look at the factor loadings in the pco object. These are the alignments (correlations) between the original attributes (loci) and the PCoA axes. Those SNP loci that load high (have a high correlation) with Axis 1 are the ones contributing most to the separation of  Variety 1 from remainder. The private alleles should be among them,

How can I retrieve the SNP loci that has been used for explaining this variation? is this information in the object created by the function gl.assign?

Thanks a lot for the help.

Kind regards,
JB

> (b) Remainder (k=28)
>
> The challenge you face is that with only n=3 replicates for each variety, you will have substantial sampling error to deal with. So any private alleles you see in your sample may be private for the varieties, or private because of sampling error. Similar considerations will plague fixed differences or comparisons of allele frequency profiles.
>
> The step that you have already taken, is,
>
> gl <- gl.reassign.pop(gl, old=c(list the 28 pops here in quotes), new='remainder')
> gl.report.pa <http://gl.report.pa>(gl)
>
> Because of the sampling error issue (n=3), I think that you should consider only private alleles that are present in  Varieties 1 and 2, and not private alleles present in 'remainder'. The latter may be private alleles present in remainder (arising from 28 instances of n=3) but absent in  Variety 1 or  Variety 2 because of sampling error (one instance of n=3 in each case).
>
> If you had a good handle of allele frequency profiles, say n=30 for each variety, then the sampling error issue would be less of a challenge and you could use assignment tests, fixed difference analysis, or filter on minor allele frequency before identifying private alleles.
>
> Another more visual approach you might try is to do a Principal Coordinates Analysis,
>
> pco <- gl.pcoa(gl)
>
> and plot the results
>
> gl.pcoa.plot(pco, gl)
>
> to see if you get good separation of  Variety 1,  Variety 2 and remainder.
>
> If  Variety 1 and remainder have good separation on PCoA1 (and good value for variance explained), then you can look at the factor loadings in the pco object. These are the alignments (correlations) between the original attributes (loci) and the PCoA axes. Those SNP loci that load high (have a high correlation) with Axis 1 are the ones contributing most to the separation of  Variety 1 from remainder. The private alleles should be among them, but this correlative approach is not an all or nothing thing. In combination, these high loading SNP loci should give a good indication of  Variety membership (visually if you plot the unknowns with the knowns).
>
> There are more targetted ways of doing this (discriminant analysis) but we have not implemented them in dartR yet. You might find them elsewhere.
>
> Also, I may not be much in advance of you in knowledge of this topic, so please take the above as suggestions only, and seek more experienced advice.
>
> All the best,
>
> A

messages.body_plain:
Hi Julio,

Kate's solution should work for you if you accept the DAPC approach. If you want to remain with PCoA, then you need to look inside the pcoa object generated by

pcoa <- gl.pcoa()

This object pcoa contains the eigenvalues, factor scores and factor loadings.

 === PCA of genlight object ===
Class: list of type glPca
Call ($call):glPca(x = x, nf = nfactors, parallel = parallel, n.cores = n.cores)

Eigenvalues ($eig):
 0.539 0.45 0.268 0.191 0.13 0.109 ...

Principal components ($scores):
 matrix with 250 rows (individuals) and 5 columns (axes)

Principal axes ($loadings):
 matrix with 255 rows (SNPs) and 5 columns (axes)

So you need to look at the vector pcoa$loadings. The SNPs that load high with PCoA axis 1 are the ones responsible for the variation seen in the direction of axis1. By loading high, i mean having a large magnitude (plus or minus). So if a SNP has a loading of +1 or -1, then it is loading very high.

Hope this helps.

A

messages.subject: Obtaining Fis and Wang relatedness measures per population - gl2demerelate conversion error
messages.subject_clean: Obtaining Fis and Wang relatedness measures per population - gl2demerelate conversion error
messages.body_plain:
Hey guys,

I am looking at population genetics and wish to obtain inbreeding co-efficient (Fis), and the Wang relatedness measure (as described in Wang 2002), for each population. It seems like the R package Demerelate would be best used to obtain these values.

I have tried to use the gl2demerelate and it initially worked in creating an object to be used in Demerelate, but when I tried to run a function it has come up with the following error message:

ggbfdeme<-gl2demerelate(ggbfil)

Demerelate(ggbfdeme, tab.dist = "NA", ref.pop = "NA",
           object = TRUE, value = "wang", Fis = TRUE,
           file.output = FALSE, p.correct = FALSE,
           iteration = 10, pairs = 10,
           dis.data = "decimal", NA.rm = TRUE,
           genotype.ref = TRUE)

"Error in heterozygotes/2 : non-numeric argument to binary operator
In addition: Warning message:
In Demerelate(ggbfdeme, tab.dist = "NA", ref.pop = "NA", object = TRUE,  :
  Careful, bi-allelic markers are detected!
  Especially, rxy and ritland estimator are not defined when bi-allelic estimates are used with allele frequencies of 0.5.
  You should consider removing bi-allelics which tend to have very evenly distributed alleles or swich to another estimator.
  Be careful even if allele frequencies are not perfectly 0.5, during randomizations problems may occur due to producing randomly such populations."

Any help or assistance in understanding what the issue is would be hugely appreciated. Perhaps there is an extra filter that I need to do before I convert the gl object object containing the DArT data into a Demerelate object?

Also, for now I have used the round-a-bout way of calculating the Fis value for each population by using the gl.basic.stats function. I exported the results of Ho and Hs to an excel file. I then averaged out the Ho and Hs for each population. I then used the equation for calculating Fis [Fis = 1-(Ho/Hs)] with the averaged Ho and Hs for each population. I have cross-compared these manual calculations in excel to the overall results that are in the summary of the gl.basic.stats function, and the results are reproducible. Is anyone able to comment if this is an appropriate way of doing this? And if so how do I go about getting standard errors or confidence intervals? (Is the most appropriate approach to calculate standard error of the Fis per loci for each population?).

And lastly, if a can't get Demerelate to work, are there any other suggestions for how I might go about obtaining Wangs relatedness numbers for each population from my DArT SNP data?

Once again, any help would be hugely appreciate! Thanks in advanced.

Kind regards,
Chad

References

Wang, J., 2002. An estimator for pairwise relatedness using molecular markers. Genetics, 160(3), pp.1203-1215.
